rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Copying vs. paraphrasing: Copying = writing the exact words from the passage (0 marks). Paraphrasing = expressing the SAME MEANING in YOUR OWN WORDS (full marks). Example: Passage says 'The children played joyfully in the garden.' Copy: 'The children played joyfully in the garden' (wrong). Paraphrase: 'The kids had fun playing outdoors in the garden' (correct).…  ·  Inference vs. opinion: An inference is a LOGICAL conclusion drawn from evidence in the passage. An opinion is YOUR PERSONAL belief that may or may not be supported by the passage. Inference: 'The character was likely anxious because she kept checking her watch.' Opinion: 'I think the character was anxious because I get nervous too.' Inferences use passage evidence; opinions…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: answer pattern for "Comprehension and Unseen Passage": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.  ·  Comprehension skills are tested in virtually every English examination worldwide — NEB, CBSE, ICSE, Cambridge IGCSE, IELTS, TOEFL. The 'locate-then-restate' method (find the answer in the text, express it in your own words) is the universal standard across all these exams.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **What it is:** extracting and restating passage information — the trap is copying whole sentences; the skill is locate-then-restate.  ·  **Method:** skim for gist → scan for the question's keywords (the answer lives nearby) → answer in complete sentences with synonyms → match the question type (WH → answer the WH; 'Why' → 'Because…'; true/false → quote evidence) → verify against the text.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: In the NEB English exam, comprehension typically carries 15-20 marks out of 60-80 total. It is the single highest-weighted section. Mastering comprehension technique can add 5-8 marks to your total score — more than any other single skill.  ·  Research by reading specialists shows that students who practice 'active reading' (predicting, questioning, visualising, summarising) score 25-30% higher on comprehension tests than students who read passively. The four strategies above (skim-scan-locate-restate) are a practical application of active reading.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: True vs. Not Given: True = the passage CONFIRMS the statement. False = the passage CONTRADICTS the statement. Not Given = the passage NEITHER confirms nor contradicts — the information is simply absent. Example: Passage says 'Rahul went to school.' Statement: 'Rahul walked to school.' This is NOT GIVEN — we know he went, but not HOW.…  ·  Short answer vs. long answer format: A short answer (1 mark) is one complete sentence that directly answers the question. A long answer (2-3 marks) is answer + evidence/reason. Format for long answers: 'The answer is X because Y [with reference to the passage].' For short answers, skip the 'because' — just state the answer directly.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The most common comprehension error across all levels is copying from the passage. Studies of examiner reports show that 40-60% of students who lose marks in comprehension do so because they copied sentences instead of paraphrasing. This single habit is the biggest barrier to high comprehension scores.  ·  Paraphrasing is a transferable skill — it is used not just in comprehension but also in summarisation, note-making, essay writing, and even in professional contexts like research and journalism. Mastering paraphrasing in exam preparation benefits your overall English proficiency.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Grammar of answers:** convert passage nouns into clauses ('its existence' → 'that it exists'); use report frames ('the passage states that…'); keep the passage's tense zone; quote marks ONLY when demanded.  ·  **Length discipline:** 1-mark answers = one sentence; 2-mark answers = answer + reason/evidence.  ·  **Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Main idea vs. topic: The TOPIC is what the passage is about (one word or phrase: 'deforestation'). The MAIN IDEA is what the passage says ABOUT the topic (a complete sentence: 'Deforestation in Nepal is accelerating due to population pressure and policy failures').…  ·  one worked example for "Comprehension and Unseen Passage" — check units / edge cases.  ·  recall card: definition → formula → limit → one error to avoid.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **The four-step comprehension method:** (1) SKIM — read the passage once quickly (60 seconds) to get the gist. Don't stop for unknown words. (2) SCAN — read the questions FIRST, then scan the passage for keywords related to each question. (3) LOCATE — find the exact sentence(s) that contain the answer. Underline them.…  ·  **Why copying is the #1 comprehension error:** Examiners explicitly penalise copied sentences. If the passage says 'The river was polluted with industrial waste,' and you write 'The river was polluted with industrial waste,' you get ZERO marks for that answer.…  ·  **Paraphrasing techniques for exam success:** (1) *Synonym swap*: 'happy' → 'joyful', 'big' → 'large', 'sad' → 'sorrowful'. (2) *Word class change*: 'The government decided' → 'The government's decision was…' (3) *Voice change*: 'They built the bridge' → 'The bridge was built by them.' (4) *Clause reduction*:…
